title: Ang 262–268: Sukhmani begins
hookLine: the psalm of peace, on the page
tomorrow: can you read the Sukhmani to get a good result?

cards: Search your own name and sometimes it turns up somewhere strange: a street sign, an old song, a boat. Simran opened the Sukhmani on Ang 262, the psalm her dad plays on long hauls, and a few lines in she stopped.
Her own name, more or less, three times in a row: simrau, simar, simar. A typo? A stutter?
Turns out it's a puzzle, and the first page solves it.

teach.b: Start at the top. The Sukhmani opens with a salok of four bows: to the primal Guru, to the Guru of the ages, to the True Guru, to the Divine Guru.
Then the first stanza, in paraphrase: I remember, and remembering, remembering, I find peace. The repetition isn't a stutter. It's the instruction, said the way you do it: again and again.
And the name Simran is that same word: remembrance, the Sikh practice of keeping God's Name in mind. Then the second odd detail.

teach.h: THE TITLE IS IN THE PAUSE.
teach.b: Where's the title? It's tucked into a short line marked rahao, which tells the singer to pause. In paraphrase: Sukhmani, peace, is the nectar of God's Name; it rests in the minds of the devotees.
A rahao line holds the hymn's center, the thought it keeps coming back to. So the Sukhmani names itself in the pause. Peace isn't announced up front like a promise.

teach.h: PEACE IS FOUND IN THE STOPPING.

teach.b: Put the two clues together and the first page tells you what to do, remember, and where you'll find what you're looking for: in the pause.
Guru Arjan's psalm runs on for many pages, and it starts as small as a name said three times.

how: Sikhs read or sing the Sukhmani at home and in the gurdwara, alone or together; its rahao line names the psalm and calls it the peace of God's Name.

o: the page where Guru Arjan's psalm of peace begins
the page where Guru Arjan's poem of letters ends
a page of the evening prayer said before sleep

games.q: the psalm's first page — tap the pairs.

s: the Sukhmani's title is in its first line
it's tucked into the rahao, the pause line: peace, the nectar of God's Name.
the first stanza repeats the word for remembering
remember, and remembering, remembering, find peace.
the opening salok bows to the Guru four ways
the primal Guru, the Guru of the ages, the True Guru, the Divine Guru.

games.q: your roommate keeps a sticky note on her mirror with one word written three times. she says repetition is "just for memorizing." what does the Sukhmani's opening suggest?
o: the repeating is the practice: remember, again and again, and find peace.
she's right; repetition is a memory trick and nothing more.
repetition only works in Gurmukhi; in English it does nothing.
games.why: simrau, simar, simar: the first stanza says the instruction the way you do it. remembering, again and again, is where the peace comes from.

practice: Say the word remember softly three times, the way the Sukhmani does, with one slow breath between each. If Waheguru is your word, say that instead.
Then stop, and stay in the pause after the third: that's where the psalm keeps its peace.

wordCard.voice: Ang 262: where the Sukhmani, Guru Arjan's psalm of peace, begins, with remembrance said three times.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: simran, remembrance of God's Name; the Sukhmani's first stanza begins with it.

carryVoice: Your line: peace begins. Not with a promise up front, but in the pause after you remember. Rest easy.

sources.ref: Ang 262 (Gauri Sukhmani, Mahala 5: the opening salok 'aad gure namah, jugaad gure namah, satgure namah, sree gurdeve namah'; the first stanza 'simrau simar simar sukh paavau'; the rahao 'sukhmanee sukh amrit prabh naam, bhagat janaa kai man bisraam'), paraphrased
